title: Common data structures and when to use them
description: Explore arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, and graphs with practical guidance.

data.text: A data structure is a format for organizing data so it can be accessed and modified efficiently. Choosing the right data structure is often more important than choosing the right algorithm. The same data can be stored in many ways, and each way changes how fast you can search, insert, delete, or iterate.

An array stores elements in a contiguous block of memory. You can jump directly to any index in O(1) time. A linked list stores elements as nodes linked by pointers. You cannot jump directly to an index — you must walk the list — but inserting or deleting at the beginning is O(1).

data.title: Use arrays for random access
data.text: If you know the index of what you need, arrays are unbeatable. Use linked lists when you frequently add or remove items from the front of a sequence.

A stack is a last-in, first-out (LIFO) structure. You push items on top and pop them from the top. A queue is a first-in, first-out (FIFO) structure. You enqueue at the back and dequeue from the front. Both can be implemented with arrays or linked lists.

data.title: Real-world analogies
items: Stack — a stack of plates: the last plate added is the first one taken
Queue — a line at a store: the first person in line is the first served
Stack use cases — undo systems, expression parsing, backtracking
Queue use cases — task scheduling, message handling, breadth-first search

data.title: Stack implementation in C#
data.content: C# provides a built-in Stack<T> class with Push and Pop methods.

data.text: A hash table stores key-value pairs and looks up values by key in O(1) average time. It uses a hash function to convert the key into an array index. Collisions — when two keys map to the same index — are handled with chaining or open addressing. In C#, Dictionary<TKey, TValue> is a hash table.

Trees organize data hierarchically. A binary search tree (BST) keeps smaller values on the left and larger values on the right, enabling fast search. A heap is a special tree used for priority queues. Graphs are collections of nodes connected by edges and model networks, relationships, and dependencies.

items.question: When should I use a linked list over an array?
items.answer: Use a linked list when you need frequent insertions or deletions in the middle of a sequence and do not need random access by index.

items.question: What is the difference between a tree and a graph?
items.answer: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. A graph can have cycles and does not require a single root node.

items.question: Are hash tables always O(1)?
items.answer: Average case is O(1), but worst case is O(n) if every key collides. Good hash functions and resizing keep collisions rare in practice.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Arrays offer fast random access but slow middle insertions
Linked lists offer fast insertions but slow random access
Hash tables give average O(1) lookup by key
Trees and graphs model hierarchical and network relationships
data.takeaway: Choose the data structure that matches your most common operation: access, insertion, deletion, or search.
